title.narrative: ROAP/PHL Transformative Actions for Climate and Ecological Protection and Development (TRANSCEND)_GIZ

description.narrative:
The Transformative Actions for Climate and Ecological Protection and Development (TRANSCEND) project aims to respond to the needs and priorities as identified in national development and investment plans such as National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP), Philippine Development Plan (PDP) and National Housing and Urban Development Sector Plan (NHUDSP) with targeted measures and an integrated landscape approach in three selected areas. This is consistent with the National Spatial Strategy where reduced vulnerability and regional agglomeration with growth in key centres and connectivity are main components. It will enhance government and stakeholder efforts in reaching its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets and goals of a post-2020 Biodiversity Framework.
On April 15th, 2021, the Republic of the Philippines, in accordance with the Decision 1/CP.21 of the 21st Conference of Parties (COP) to the UNFCCC, submitted its NDCs towards addressing climate change. In its 2021 NDC, the government committed to a projected GHG emissions reduction and avoidance of 75%, of which 2.71% is unconditional and 72.9% is conditional on external finance from 2020 to 2030. The commitment covers agriculture, waste, industry, transport, and energy sectors. The Philippines maintains an active role in the UNFCCC and CBD and has always actively shared country experience. The project will ensure that knowledge products and outcome documents draw from learning and innovations and make use of collaboration platforms.
The Philippines has been identified as fourth in the world in terms of long-term climate risk over 20 years, according to Germany’s Climate Risk Index . The increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events pose increasing challenges. The population of the Philippines is growing and the percentage of people living in urban areas has consistently increased disproportionally. In 2020, the number of people living in urban areas had reached nearly 47.5%, a spectacular increase of 16 million in a span of a decade making it the second-highest average urban density in East Asia and the Pacific. With this urbanization context, cities and settlements in the Philippines are crucial for delivering ecological and climate protection. Cities and human settlements, offers the opportunity to implement sustainable solutions that maximizes the competitive advantage of putting value on the direct use, indirect use, option to use and non-use of environment and natural resources alongside identified “grey” interventions for climate resilience and ecological stability.
The government has developed policies and initiatives to respond to these challenges. They promote a ridge-to-reef approach in addressing climate change which gives premium to the urban-rural continuum in ecological landscapes to deliver sustainable solutions. However, national and local governments still need further support to effectively implement transformative solutions given limitations in capacities and policies.
Resilient communities and built environment:
Rapid unplanned urbanisation increases exposure to the impacts of climate change, e.g. through settlements on flood plains, and can lead to higher Green House Gas (GHG) emissions, e.g. through poor building standards. low energy efficiency in the buildings, industry and commercial sectors contribute to GHG emissions. Moreover, vulnerability of the power sector has not been assessed yet.
The government’s National Urban Development and Housing Framework (NUDHF) and the actions identified in the National Housing and Urban Development Sector Plan 2040 particularly outline the need of making ‘climate resilience’ as a base for urban planning and investments. While these policy issuances provide clear entry points to facilitate transformative climate actions in the built environment setting, there is a need to introduce ecosystem-based adaptation as part of the main considerations. While using technological and built infrastructural interventions, at the same time nature-based solutions and local knowledge bases, ecologies, and processes need to be considered.
Government planning policies and guidelines, as well as the Climate Change Act, mandate LGUs to formulate their local climate action plans and integrate the actions into the wider spatial and sectoral development plans of local governments. While 82% of the total LGUs in the country have formulated their climate action plans, gaps and constraints still abound in delivering desired adaptation and co-benefits to GHG emission reduction. Understanding and use of ecosystem-services for urban and built environment adaptation is often missing and not explored. Mainly such is due to the fragmentation in climate planning, limitation in tools, and gaps in the planning policy issuances and guidance on urban EbA.
